story_text.value:
Shipped Beeline today. It's a team chat for humans and agents - a kind of multiplayer harness. You can bring your codex, Claude code, opencode subscriptions and also works with pi and goose. We built beeline itself with early versions of beeline, and use it to build our other projects - it's boosted productivity quite a bit for us.

Demo video: https://youtu.be/ACdelpZC2z4?is=pP6MFxJODvKcGjQt

The key insight is that humans do their best work in teams, but agentic development has so far been single player. This has led to people having to forward AI slop to each other or to try to deliver context through various shims like meetings or task tickets.

Beeline is a single control plane for your entire team, both human and agent, and is designed to help your team do its best work.

Things to expect: - This is a multiplayer agentic harness, not a slack substitute. It's best for focused product teams doing or relying on engineering tools and shipping code. - Open source and not a business. We use beeline internally, and just thought it would be a really cool thing to exist in the world. There are still lots of bugs - Sweepstakes things like computer use, lots of third party connector integrations are there. What's cool is that beeline agents can automate _auth_ through trustysquire.ai - they can sign up to most services and APIs without you having to do it for them. - A new primitive called workflows, that are skills for teams of agents. - multi way call with your entire team, humans and agents. I like it quite a bit.

Looking forward to feedback!

story_text.value:
when I started using coding agents heavily, they began creating tons of Git worktrees. different tools like Codex, Claude Code, T3 Code, Orca, Superset, and others all put their worktrees in different directories, which made them pretty hard to find.

I know you can just ask an agent to find them, and a lot of people do exactly that. but I wanted a deterministic solution that wouldn't depend on an agent getting things right or waste extra tokens.

so.. I built Lopper!

it's a tool that searches for git repositories and worktrees across different directories on your machine and shows them all in one place in a TUI, where you can inspect them and remove the ones you no longer need. it also has a CLI for scripts and agents, so they can manage worktrees more reliably.

would you use something like this? what am I missing compared to just asking an agent to handle it?

story_text.value:
I build websites for a living. Lately, it's more about prompting than actually writing the code (the art part is still there). So I decided to leave that part to Claude too and see what it would come up with. So far, I have given it

- A baseline website - Full access to Google, X, LinkedIn and Reddit Ads, with a budget - Apify access - Openrouter access

I also wanted it to personalize the website completely based on the user. No 2 users see the same website, most of the content is rendered on the client side using Deepseek. It uses - Device (GPU model, battery percentage, fonts installed, resolution, adblock installed, camera and mic connected, mouse polling rate, scroll speed, etc) - Demographics (Weather, time of the day, news around you, ..) - Behavior (Scroll speed, clicks, selection, referrer, etc) - Tons of other connected services through Apify

So far it's doing tomfoolery for the most part. Like creating a gazzilion pages for SEO (exactly what our interns say every time), trying to go viral by adding share buttons, etc. But it's still super fun to see it make decisions every 4 hours.

story_text.value:
I started Stylebot in 2010 to change how websites look without writing CSS by hand. I have kept maintaining it since then. Now, with AI tools, I’ve finally been able to fix bugs and add features I never had time for.

4.0 has a new, modern editor that shows each element's actual styles, profiles, better sync, versioning and includes a CLI for coding agents.

I am most excited about adding the CLI, which lets claude code or any other agent restyle any webpage in your real browser and check its work with screenshots. It lets me restyle webpages quite dramatically using coding agents. For example, you can see the example newspaper-style HN themes: https://stylebot.dev/#gallery

It's free and open source in Chrome, Edge and Firefox (Safari coming soon!). Code: https://github.com/ankit/stylebot

I'd love to hear ideas and suggestions. My plan is to add a Stylebot Gallery next, which would let users share and install creations from other other users. I also plan to make improvements so its more resilient to website and CSS changes. Thank you!

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I built Nexus because I was tired of having multiple agents that I had to address one by one. I built an underlying mechanism where I could message all of them and have them have the capability to message each other and listen to wake events. I also got tired of having to run cron when I think that agents should have the capability to be event-driven.

Nexus is basically a daemon that runs and routes messages to where they need to be, it is fully customizable, which you can write scripts off of so that it will wake agents or route that message to an already existing agent. Right now it supports Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode and Hermes. But more are underway. It runs on your machine with no container required. (In my opinion, messaging within your machine should not require you to have to run a container.)

To try it:

  npm install --global @egregore/nexus
It runs on Linux, Windows and WSL today; It can run on mac but I havent fully tested it also you would have to build the binaries yourself for the latest version though. Full support for it is planned in the near future.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm the author. FACE is a single Go binary. You run `face` in the folder that holds your projects and it serves a page on 127.0.0.1. It speaks ACP (the Agent Client Protocol that Zed published) to the official CLI of the agent you already use: Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Cursor, OpenCode, Qwen Code or Antigravity, signed in with your own account. FACE has no model, no key and no agent loop of its own.

Why I built it: a coding agent ships a feature in an afternoon, and three people and five sessions later nobody can answer "what is in flight, what did it cost, why was it decided this way". The answer I landed on is not a dashboard but a method where every decision and every delivery is a versioned file: a handful of docs written once, a queue with one line per delivery (docs/06), and one page per delivery (work/<slug>.md) that says what will be built and how it is proven before any code changes. The method is four slash commands the agent reads from one file (brainstorm, analyze, propose, apply); it works without FACE. FACE is the window: the queue becomes a five-lane board, a card opens into the page plus the live session, and the commit window shows exactly what the agent staged. The agent never commits or merges; you click.

I built FACE itself with it, from the fourth week on. Before that the same method shipped a job marketplace in 89 one-page deliveries over 14 days, and a consulting project in 107 deliveries over 19 days.

Install: `brew install jckodel/face/face`, `winget install JCKodel.FACE`, a `.deb`, or `curl -fsSL https://face.kodel.com.br/install.sh | sh`. macOS, Linux, Windows, arm64 and amd64. UI in en, pt, es, fr, de and zh-Hans.

What is missing: single user and local only (a team mode with a server on your network is the next milestone); no editor (it shows code and diffs, your editor stays your editor); the source is not public yet. It will be visible under a fair source license when the paid tier for teams exists, and the free tier stays free. By itself FACE makes at most two requests, both off until you turn them on: a daily anonymous ping that counts machines and a daily version check. The page "What FACE sends" lists both URLs.

Happy to answer anything about ACP, the adapters for Claude and Codex (they are not ACP native, so FACE wraps them), or the method.

title.value: Show HN: Face, a browser window over agents that keeps the plan in files

story_text.value:
So I've been working on a project (Make0 AI) for a long time where I wanted to give common context to both Codex and Claude Code. The problem is simple - while working on Claude and after exhausting the daily/weekly limits I've start again from scratch in Codex. Of course I can prompt Claude to summarise a handoff that I can give to Codex but that is inefficient. So I thought of a creating a common context for both of them locally using a simple list of instructions like a shared md file. But the problem was the file kept on growing and after some point the common context went beyond 20k tokens and was just inflating the token budget unnecessarily.

Then I implemented a RAG based retrieval approach on the list to only load what is required for that prompt and voila, after a few more iterations it resulted into a graph memory - Brain.

So this product Make0 AI gives you the ability to create Brains that you can connect to any Ai agent via MCP and then they immediately know your likes, dislikes, preferences etc. AI agents can read, write to this memory.

This can be your long term memory and the agents just become the token providers and task executors. You have full control over your data/memories from a single place. Think of this as a "USB thumb drive brain" that you plug to any agent.

I know I may not be the first one to implement this but I tried to make the UX simple and is not at all developer focused. You can just drag and drop your memories/data to the brain and even play around with a visual brain.

One more thing, i've done benchmarks on the memory. LoCoMo scores 83.3% overall, with Single hop 92.5% in standard mode (available now) and in another configuration (experimental max mode) it scores 92% overall and 94.4% in single hop. Available in the benchmark page. It uses hybrid search + graph memory and has built in conflict resolution for memories.

Do let me know if you folks wanna try it!

title.value: Show HN: Working on Plug and play AI memory that works across AI agents

story_text.value:
I use Claude Code inside VS Code, and four things kept getting in my way:

1. I couldn't send Claude my Markdown Editor selection, or a file I had open as a preview. 2. The claude CLI got none of the editor's context. 3. Claude couldn't run VS Code commands, so it couldn't adapt VS Code to what I was doing. 4. File links in its chat ignored the editor I chose for the file type and opened as raw text (https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/81482).

So I wrote an extension and a Claude Code plugin that fix those. It turned out useful enough to share.
